title: DNA & RNA Concentration Calculator + A260 Self-Test
description: Enter your A260 for dsDNA, ssDNA or RNA and get ng/µL with the 260/280 and 260/230 purity ratios, then test yourself on six questions about them.
intro: Six questions on the numbers a NanoDrop hands you: which factor goes with which nucleic acid, what each purity ratio catches, and where the dilution factor belongs.

questions.q: Which factor does this page use for RNA, and why is it not the dsDNA one?
options: 33 µg/mL, since RNA is single-stranded like ssDNA
40 µg/mL, since its bases are more exposed
50 µg/mL, the same factor used for dsDNA
20 µg/mL, because RNA absorbs at 230 nm
questions.why: RNA converts at 40 rather than ssDNA's 33 or dsDNA's 50, so being single-stranded is not by itself what sets the factor.
questions.source: Page factors: FACTOR={dsDNA:50, ssDNA:33, RNA:40}, stated in 'How the numbers work' as 50 µg/mL dsDNA, 33 µg/mL ssDNA, 40 µg/mL RNA at A260 = 1.0, 1 cm path.

questions.q: Which contamination does the 260/280 ratio flag, in the way this page splits the two ratios?
options: Protein or phenol, which absorb at 280 nm
Guanidine salts, which absorb near 230 nm
Carbohydrates carried over from extraction
EDTA left behind in the elution buffer
questions.why: 260/280 is the protein and phenol check, while guanidine, carbohydrate and EDTA carryover shows up in 260/230 instead.
questions.source: Page ratio table: 260/280 low means 'Residual protein or phenol (they absorb at 280 nm)'; 260/230 low means 'Chaotropic salts (guanidine), phenol, carbohydrates, EDTA (absorb at 230 nm)'.

questions.q: An RNA prep reads 260/280 = 2.00, which the page calls clean, but its 260/230 is 1.40. Most likely cause?
options: Protein carryover, which absorbs strongly at 230 nm
Nothing, since 1.40 is the target for this ratio
Guanidine salt, phenol or carbohydrate carryover
Too much RNA, so the reading ran past the range
questions.why: The two ratios catch different problems, so a prep can pass 260/280 and still show leftover extraction reagents in a low 260/230.
questions.source: Page: 260/230 clean is ~2.0 to 2.2, and the tool labels r<1.8 as 'low, salt, phenol, carbohydrate, or EDTA carryover'. 1.40 < 1.8, so it is flagged low.

questions.q: You diluted the sample 1:20 before reading A260 = 0.300. How does the dilution factor enter?
options: Divide the A260 by 20 before applying the factor
It does not enter, the reading self-corrects
Divide the final concentration by 20 at the end
Multiply A260 by the factor and then by 20
questions.why: A260 describes the diluted sample, so the dilution factor multiplies the result to get back to the stock concentration.
questions.source: Page formula: conc = A260 × factor × dilution. Worked example does 0.400 × 50 × 50 = 1000 ng/µL, multiplying by the dilution rather than dividing.

questions.q: Take the worked example's A260 = 0.400 at a 1:50 dilution, but the sample is RNA, not dsDNA. Concentration?
options: 660 ng/µL
1000 ng/µL
800 ng/µL
16 ng/µL
questions.why: Only the factor changes when the sample type changes, so swapping 50 for RNA's 40 scales the same reading down by one fifth.
questions.source: 0.400 × 40 × 50 = 800 ng/µL. Distractors: 0.400 × 50 × 50 = 1000 (dsDNA factor kept), 0.400 × 33 × 50 = 660 (ssDNA factor), 0.400 × 40 = 16 (dilution forgotten).

questions.q: Same worked example, A260 = 0.400, but A280 comes back 0.250. What is the 260/280 and how does the page read it?
options: 1.60, low, so protein or phenol shows
1.60, within the clean DNA band near 1.8
1.60, high, so RNA carryover is flagged
1.80, the ideal value for clean DNA prep
questions.why: The ratio is A260 divided by A280, and 1.60 falls under the 1.7 floor this page uses for DNA, which points at protein or phenol.
questions.source: 0.400 / 0.250 = 1.60. Page logic for DNA: clean if r >= 1.70 and r <= 1.95, otherwise r < 1.70 gives 'low, likely protein or phenol contamination' and r > 1.95 gives the RNA-carryover warning.
